attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, listed among his 'dark predictions'.

semantics.note: Firm 'will' forecast with an 'eventually' horizon. The normalised text drops 'be able to', turning a prediction about capability into a prediction that bad actors actually do it. The contract restores the capability reading, so scoring under the contract is unaffected.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary and fair: copying means functional imitation of original-GPT-4-level ability, it predicts available capability rather than actual deployment, and it does not require flawless execution. The contract also rules out contradiction from mere absence.

evidence.note: Dated June 2024. In Table 4's baseline rows, Llama 3 70B Instruct matches or beats GPT-4-0613 on MT Bench, AlpacaEval and Arena Hard. This establishes an openly available model with GPT-4-like language ability.

Dated July 2024. Safeguards were removed from Llama 3 70B with minimal loss on capability benchmarks, and disinformation-category attack success rose from 40% to about 94–97%. This is the same model as in e1.

Same study. The authors warn that attack success measures attempts to comply, not output quality. They call the unsafe outputs reasonably good on inspection but did not quantify quality. This limits claims about narrative reliability.

reviews.rationale: The early-resolution rule is met by dated 2024 evidence. An open-weight Llama 3 70B performs comparably to GPT-4-0613 (e1), and its safeguards were removed cheaply while it kept its capabilities and complied with nearly all disinformation requests (e2). The caveat about output quality (e3) limits how reliable 'whatever narratives' can be shown to be, but the contract does not require perfect execution.
